title: Entanglement, built by hand
summary: Two gates make two qubits share one fate. Build a Bell state and see what entanglement does — and doesn't — do.

shots.title:
Two qubits,
one state.
shots.subtitle: Entanglement is what makes many qubits more than many coins.
shots.narration: One qubit is interesting. Two qubits are where quantum computing really starts.

frames.caption: Two qubits need four amplitudes. Start: |00⟩
H on the first qubit: |00⟩ and |10⟩, half each
CNOT: the first qubit flips the second → |00⟩ and |11⟩

shots.narration: Two qubits need four amplitudes, one per combination. Start in zero zero. A Hadamard on the first qubit splits it into zero zero and one zero. Then a controlled NOT flips the second qubit whenever the first is one.
As a circuit it's just two gates: H, then a CNOT. The result is a Bell state: half zero zero, half one one, and never anything else.

shots.text: Measure either qubit: a **random** 0 or 1. Measure both: they **always agree**.
shots.narration: Measure either qubit alone and you get a perfectly random bit. Measure both and they always agree. That shared randomness is entanglement.

shots.text: Neither qubit has a state of its own any more. Only the **pair** does.
shots.narration: Here's the strange part. Neither qubit has a state of its own any more. You can only describe the pair. In the lab you'll see each qubit's Bloch vector shrink to nothing.

shots.text: Entanglement creates correlations, not messages. It can't send information **faster than light** — or front-run a market.
shots.narration: And a myth to bury. Entanglement creates correlations, not messages. It cannot send information faster than light, so it cannot be used to front-run a market across the ocean.

shots.text: Why it matters: algorithms use entanglement to make **wrong answers interfere away** across many qubits at once.
shots.narration: What it is good for: algorithms use entanglement and interference across many qubits, so that amplitudes of wrong answers cancel and right answers reinforce.

steps.title: Build a Bell state
steps.brief: Pick a gate from the palette and click a cell to place it. For CNOT (●⊕), click the control qubit, then the target. Hit the target state, run some shots, then save it to your notebook.

steps.title: The same circuit in Quirk
steps.caption: Quirk is a free, open-source circuit simulator by Craig Gidney. Here is the Bell circuit you just built — drag in more gates and watch the state displays update.

questions.prompt: You measure the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. Which outcomes can occur?
questions.explain: The two qubits always agree: half the time 00, half the time 11.

questions.prompt: Can entanglement be used to send a trading signal faster than light?
options: Yes, that's how quantum networks work
No — it creates correlations, not messages
questions.explain: Each side alone sees random results; you still need a classical channel to compare them.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that create the Bell state from |00⟩.
items: Apply H to the first qubit
Apply CNOT with the first qubit as control
questions.explain: Superpose first, then entangle with the CNOT.
